Advice about stitches, piles, bleeding and other physical changes after birth, plus tips to help you make a healthy recovery.
If you've had a caesarean, see recovering from a caesarean .
Stitches — If you've had stitches after tearing or an episiotomy (cut) , bathe them every day to help prevent infection. Have a bath or shower with plain warm water then carefully pat yourself dry.
Stitches — If your stitches are sore or uncomfortable, tell your midwife.
Stitches — Painkillers can help. If you're breastfeeding, check with a pharmacist, midwife or GP before you buy over-the-counter painkillers.
Stitches — Stitches usually dissolve by the time the cut or tear has healed, but sometimes they have to be taken out.
Going to the toilet — At first, the thought of peeing can be a bit frightening – because of the soreness. Drinking lots of water dilutes your urine, which may make it sting less.
Going to the toilet — Tell your midwife if:
Going to the toilet — you're finding it really difficult to pee
Going to the toilet — you feel very sore
Going to the toilet — you notice an unpleasant smell
Going to the toilet — You probably won't have a poo for a few days after the birth, but it's important not to let yourself get constipated .
Going to the toilet — Eat plenty of fresh fruit, vegetables, salad, wholegrain cereals and wholemeal bread, and drink plenty of water.
Going to the toilet — If you've had stitches, it's very unlikely you'll break them, or open up the cut or tear again.
Going to the toilet — It might feel better if you hold a pad of clean tissue over the stitches when pooing. Try not to strain.
Going to the toilet — Talk to your midwife or GP if you have constipation that won't go away. A gentle laxative may help.
Going to the toilet — Also tell your midwife or GP if poo is leaking or you're pooing when you don't mean to.
Bladder control — After having a baby, it's quite common to leak a bit of pee if you laugh, cough or move suddenly.
Bladder control — Pelvic floor exercises can help with this but tell the GP at your postnatal check if they aren't. They may refer you to a physiotherapist.
Bladder control — Find out more about your post-pregnancy body, including how to do pelvic floor exercise .
Piles — Piles (haemorrhoids) are very common after birth but usually disappear within a few days or weeks.
Piles — Eat plenty of fresh fruit, vegetables, salad, wholegrain cereals and wholemeal bread, and drink plenty of water. This should make pooing easier and less painful.
Piles — Try not to push or strain – this will make the piles worse.
Piles — Talk to a midwife or pharmacist if you feel very uncomfortable. They can recommend creams and ointments that soothe piles.

Bleeding after birth (lochia) — You'll bleed from your vagina after the birth. It will be quite heavy at first, and you'll need super-absorbent period pads. Change them regularly, washing your hands before and afterwards.
Bleeding after birth (lochia) — It isn't a good idea to use tampons until after your 6-week postnatal check because they could increase your chance of getting an infection.

Bleeding after birth (lochia) — You may notice the bleeding is redder and heavier when you breastfeed. This happens because breastfeeding makes your womb contract. You may also feel cramps similar to period pains.
Bleeding after birth (lochia) — The bleeding will carry on for a few weeks. It will gradually turn a brownish colour and decrease until it finally stops.
Bleeding after birth (lochia) — If you're losing blood in large clots, tell your midwife. You may need some treatment.
When will my periods start again after pregnancy? — When will my periods start again after pregnancy?
When will my periods start again after pregnancy? — It's hard to be exact about when your periods will start again, as everyone is different.

When will my periods start again after pregnancy? — If you bottle feed your baby, or combine bottle feeding with breastfeeding, your first period could start as soon as 5 to 6 weeks after you give birth.
When will my periods start again after pregnancy? — If you fully breastfeed (including at night) without any bottle feeding, your periods may not start again until you start to reduce breastfeeding.
How soon after giving birth can I get pregnant? — You can get pregnant again just 3 weeks after the birth of your baby, even if you're breastfeeding and your periods have not started again yet.

How soon after giving birth can I get pregnant? — It's important to start using contraception within 21 days of giving birth to avoid a new pregnancy. Talk to your midwife or GP about a method that's best for you.
How soon after giving birth can I get pregnant? — Find out more about choosing a method of contraception .

How soon can I use tampons after giving birth? — You should not use tampons until you've had your 6-week postnatal check . This is because you'll still have a wound where the placenta joined with the wall of your womb, and you may also have tears or cuts in or around your vagina.
How soon can I use tampons after giving birth? — Using internal period products like tampons and menstrual cups before this wound has healed could increase your chance of getting an infection.
How soon can I use tampons after giving birth? — Use maternity or period pads during this time while your body is still healing.
Breasts — To begin with, your breasts will produce a yellowish liquid called colostrum for your baby.
Breasts — On the third or fourth day, they may feel tight and tender as they start to produce milk.
Breasts — Wearing a supportive nursing bra may help. Speak to your midwife if you're very uncomfortable.
Breasts — Read more about breastfeeding in the first few days .
Tummy — After delivery, your tummy will probably still be a lot bigger than before pregnancy. This is partly because your muscles have stretched.
Tummy — If you eat a balanced diet and get some exercise, your shape should gradually return.
Tummy — Breastfeeding helps because it makes your womb contract. You may feel quite painful period-like cramps while you're feeding.
Tummy — Find out more about your post-pregnancy body, including exercises to help separated stomach muscles .
Is it something serious? — Tell your midwife, health visitor or GP straight away if you get any of these symptoms.
Is it something serious? — Pain, swelling or redness in the calf muscle of one leg (but redness can be harder to see on brown and black skin)
Is it something serious? — deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
Is it something serious? — Pain in your chest, difficulty breathing
Is it something serious? — pulmonary embolism
Is it something serious? — Sudden or very heavy blood loss from your vagina, possibly feeling faint, rapid heartbeat
Is it something serious? — postpartum haemorrhage
Is it something serious? — High temperature, sore and tender tummy
Is it something serious? — Headache, changes in your vision, vomiting
Is it something serious? — pre-eclampsia

Symptoms of jaundice in babies — The main symptom of jaundice in babies is their eyes or skin look yellow.
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — You may notice yellow:
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — in the whites of their eyes
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — on their skin – this usually starts on the face and head and can spread to the rest of the body
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — under their tongue or inside their cheeks
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — The yellow can be easier to see in bright light or sunlight. Pressing gently on the tip of your baby’s nose or forehead may also make the yellow easier to see.
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — It can be harder to see yellow on black or brown skin.
Symptoms of jaundice in babies — For most babies with jaundice, the yellow is most noticeable when they’re around 3 days old. It usually takes around 2 weeks for the jaundice to go.

Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP or midwife appointment or call NHS 111 if: — Your baby is over 24 hours old and:
Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP or midwife appointment or call NHS 111 if: — you think they have jaundice
Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP or midwife appointment or call NHS 111 if: — they’ve been diagnosed with jaundice and it’s not getting better, or is getting worse

Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP or midwife appointment or call NHS 111 if: — their pee is dark yellow or brown or their poo is a pale creamy colour (keep a sample of poo to show a midwife or doctor)
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — Your baby has jaundice and:
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — is sleepier than normal or difficult to wake
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — is not feeding
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — is floppy or stiff, or they have jerking or twitching movements
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — has a high temperature of 38C or more, or a low temperature of 36C or less, feels hot or cold to the touch, or is shivering
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — has not been producing any wet nappies
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — has difficulty breathing (you may notice grunting noises or their stomach sucking in under their ribcage), is breathless or breathing very fast
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — is less than 24 hours old
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: — Bring any medicines your baby takes with you.

Causes of jaundice in babies — Jaundice in babies is usually caused when a newborn baby’s liver is not able to work properly immediately. This can cause a build-up of a waste product called bilirubin, which is usually removed from the body by the liver.
Causes of jaundice in babies — After a few weeks, the baby’s liver should develop fully and bilirubin levels will return to normal.
Causes of jaundice in babies — Other causes of newborn jaundice include:
Causes of jaundice in babies — being born with Gilbert’s syndrome , which is a common and usually harmless condition that causes episodes of jaundice
Causes of jaundice in babies — infections such as rubella (german measles)
Causes of jaundice in babies — the baby having a different blood type from their mother – haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)
Causes of jaundice in babies — problems with how a baby’s liver works
Causes of jaundice in babies — In most babies, jaundice is not a sign of another health condition.
Diagnosing jaundice in babies — Your baby will be regularly checked for signs of jaundice by your care team in the first few days after they’re born.
Diagnosing jaundice in babies — If they show signs of jaundice, their bilirubin levels will be measured. This can be done using a blood test or by pressing a special light on their skin.
Diagnosing jaundice in babies — Other tests can be used if the jaundice could be caused by something serious, like an infection or liver problems.
Diagnosing jaundice in babies — These tests can include:
Diagnosing jaundice in babies — blood tests
Diagnosing jaundice in babies — ultrasound scans of your baby’s liver
Treatment for jaundice in babies — Most babies with jaundice usually get better without treatment.
Treatment for jaundice in babies — Encouraging your baby to feed regularly, around 8 to 12 times a day, can help them get better more quickly. If they’re sleepy, try waking them for feeds.
Treatment for jaundice in babies — Ask your midwife or GP for advice if you’re finding it difficult to feed your baby, or you’re not sure they are feeding enough
Treatment for jaundice in babies — If your baby needs treatment, this is usually phototherapy.

Treatment for jaundice in babies — Phototherapy involves shining a special light on their skin. It’s usually done while your baby is lying in a cot in hospital, but sometimes you may be given equipment you can use at home.
Treatment for jaundice in babies — Most babies need around 48 hours of phototherapy.
Treatment for jaundice in babies — Rarely, your baby may need a blood transfusion or medicine into a vein. This is done in hospital.

Symptoms of nappy rash — Symptoms of nappy rash can include:
Symptoms of nappy rash — red or raw patches on your baby's bottom or the whole nappy area
Symptoms of nappy rash — spots, pimples, or blisters on your baby's bottom (spots can appear red or brown, but may be harder to see on brown and black skin)
Symptoms of nappy rash — scaly and dry skin
Symptoms of nappy rash — an itchy or painful bottom
Symptoms of nappy rash — your baby seeming uncomfortable or distressed

Things you can do to help with nappy rash — Nappy rash can be treated and prevented by following some simple advice.
Do — change wet or dirty nappies as soon as possible
Do — keep the skin clean and dry – pat or rub the skin gently to dry it
Do — leave nappies off when possible
Do — use extra absorbent nappies
Do — use dry nappy liners and change them often, if using reusable cloth nappies
Do — make sure your baby's nappies fit properly
Do — clean your baby's skin with water or fragrance-free and alcohol-free baby wipes
Do — bath your baby daily (but not more than twice a day, as washing too much can make the skin dry out)
Don’t — do not use soaps, baby lotion or bubble bath as they can irritate the skin
Don’t — do not use talcum powder or antiseptic creams or lotions on nappy rash
Don’t — do not put nappies on too tightly as it can irritate the skin
Don’t — do not use plastic underwear or nappy covers over nappies
A pharmacist can help with nappy rash — If the rash is causing your baby discomfort, a pharmacist can recommend a nappy rash cream or medicine to treat it at home.
A pharmacist can help with nappy rash — They may suggest using a thin layer of a barrier cream at each nappy change to protect the skin.
When and where to get medical help — Most symptoms of nappy rash are not serious, but sometimes you'll need to get them checked.
Non-urgent advice: See a health visitor or GP if: — your baby's nappy rash does not go away, gets worse or spreads to other areas
Non-urgent advice: See a health visitor or GP if: — your baby has a high temperature
Non-urgent advice: See a health visitor or GP if: — your baby seems very uncomfortable
Treatment for nappy rash — A GP may prescribe treatment if your baby is in a lot of discomfort or they think your baby might have an infection.
Treatment for nappy rash — They may prescribe:
Treatment for nappy rash — a steroid cream or ointment to help with redness and soreness
Treatment for nappy rash — an antifungal cream, if they think your baby has a thrush infection
Treatment for nappy rash — antibiotics, if they think your baby has a bacterial infection
Causes of nappy rash — It's normal for babies to sometimes get nappy rash.
Causes of nappy rash — It can be caused by:
Causes of nappy rash — your baby's skin being in contact with pee or poo for a long time
Causes of nappy rash — not cleaning the nappy area or changing the nappy often enough
Causes of nappy rash — the nappy rubbing against your baby's skin
Causes of nappy rash — an allergic reaction to soap, detergent or bubble bath
Causes of nappy rash — irritation from fragranced baby wipes or wipes containing alcohol
Causes of nappy rash — your baby having diarrhoea, or having a condition that makes them poo more often
Causes of nappy rash — some types of nappy made with materials that are not absorbent (do not easily soak up pee or poo), or not breathable
Causes of nappy rash — some types of medicines, such as antibiotics or laxatives (used to make it easier for your baby to poo)
Causes of nappy rash — thrush (a fungal infection)
Having a baby changes your body. Here’s some advice to help you feel comfortable with your body.
Physical problems after pregnancy — There may be physical problems after having a baby.
Physical problems after pregnancy — They can be related to pregnancy or birth, or the things you do while caring for young children, such as lifting and bending.

Physical problems after pregnancy — For some problems, you can do a lot to help yourself. For example, if you have a leaky bladder (incontinence) or a heavy feeling between your vagina and anus, you may need to strengthen the muscles around your bladder by doing pelvic floor exercises.
Physical problems after pregnancy — Also, if you have back pain , you may need to learn how to look after your back and do some exercises to strengthen it.
Physical problems after pregnancy — If a physical problem is bothering you, ask a GP or health visitor for help at any time. They can advise you and refer you to a specialist if necessary.

Your postnatal check — Your postnatal check at around 6 to 8 weeks after the birth of your baby is a good time to talk to the GP about any physical or mental health problems you've had since the birth.
Your postnatal check — Find out more about what happens at your postnatal check

Separated stomach muscles — It's common for the 2 muscles that run down the middle of your stomach to separate during pregnancy – usually about 2 finger widths. This is called diastasis recti, or divarication.
Separated stomach muscles — The amount of separation can vary. It happens because your growing womb (uterus) pushes the muscles apart, making them longer and weaker.
Separated stomach muscles — The separation between your stomach muscles will usually go back to normal by the time your baby is 8 weeks old.
Separated stomach muscles — After you have had your baby, you can check the size of the separation with this simple technique:
Separated stomach muscles — Lie on your back with your legs bent and your feet flat on the floor.
Separated stomach muscles — Raise your shoulders off the floor slightly and look down at your tummy.

Separated stomach muscles — Using the tips of your fingers, feel between the edges of the muscles, above and below your belly button. See how many fingers you can fit into the gap between your muscles.
Separated stomach muscles — Do this regularly to check that the gap is gradually getting smaller.
Separated stomach muscles — If the gap is still obvious 8 weeks after the birth, contact the GP as you may be at risk of back problems. Some women also have abdominal pain or discomfort.
Separated stomach muscles — The GP can refer you to a physiotherapist, who will give you some specific exercises to do.

Separated stomach muscles — Regular pelvic floor and deep stomach muscle exercises can help to reduce the size of the separation between your stomach muscles. It's also important to stand up tall and be aware of your posture.
Separated stomach muscles — Try to avoid exercises such as sit-ups, planks and high-impact exercises to start with. Also avoid straining on the toilet and heavy lifting.

Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Pelvic floor muscle exercises strengthen the muscles around your bladder, vagina and bottom. This can help to stop incontinence, improve prolapse and make sex better too.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — You can do these exercises lying down, sitting or standing. With practice, they can be done anywhere and at any time:
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Squeeze and draw in your bottom as if you're holding in wind.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Squeeze around your vagina and bladder (urethra) as if you're stopping the flow of urine or squeezing during intercourse.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Long squeezes – hold for as long as you can, but no longer than 10 seconds, then relax.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Short squeezes – quickly squeeze the muscles and then let them go immediately. Do this until your muscles get tired.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Aim to build up to 10 repeats of each exercise, at least 3 times a day.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — It's important to keep breathing normally while you do these exercises. Make sure you do not pull in your stomach when you squeeze.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — Sitting on the toilet can be a good reminder to do your exercises. Just make sure you do them after you've finished.
Pelvic floor muscle exercises — The Chartered Society of Physiotherapists website has a video about how to do pelvic floor exercises to help strengthen your pelvic floor
Stomach exercise — This exercise can help you tone your stomach muscles:
Stomach exercise — Lie on your side with your knees slightly bent.
Stomach exercise — Let your tummy relax and breathe in gently.
Stomach exercise — As you breathe out, gently draw in the lower part of your stomach like a corset, narrowing your waistline.
Stomach exercise — Squeeze your pelvic floor muscles at the same time.
Stomach exercise — Hold for a count of 10, breathing normally, then gently release.
Stomach exercise — Repeat up to 10 times.
Ways to ease back pain — These practical tips may help to relieve an aching back:

Ways to ease back pain — while feeding your baby, sit with your back well supported and straight. Put a small pillow or cushion behind your waist to support your lower back. Make sure your feet can reach the floor
Ways to ease back pain — kneel or squat (do not bend your back) to do tasks that are near the floor, such as picking up toys or bathing your baby
Ways to ease back pain — change a nappy on a raised surface. You could kneel on the floor next to a sofa or bed. Never leave your baby unattended on a raised surface, in case they fall off
Ways to ease back pain — keep your back straight and bend your knees when lifting
Ways to ease back pain — keep your back straight when you push your pram or buggy. Or, carry your baby in a well-fitting sling

Tips for your birthing partner or partners — Whoever you pick to be your birth partner (if you choose to have one), their job is to support, comfort and encourage you during labour and birth.
10 tips for birth partners — Here are some useful tips to share with your birth partner.
10 tips for birth partners — You could help write the birth plan, but if not, make sure you know what it says so you can support your partner during labour.
10 tips for birth partners — Be aware that birth plans often change at the last minute.
10 tips for birth partners — Read about what happens during labour and birth.
10 tips for birth partners — Going to the antenatal classes will really help - you'll learn about the signs of labour, contractions, pain relief options, what happens after birth, and lots more.
10 tips for birth partners — Make sure you know the best route to the hospital or birth centre.
10 tips for birth partners — Check how long the journey will take, and bear in mind the traffic at different times of the day.
10 tips for birth partners — If possible, avoid roads with speed bumps or train tracks. Familiarise yourself with the car park, download the parking app, or have plenty of coins in the car.
10 tips for birth partners — You need to be ready during the weeks leading up to the due date.
10 tips for birth partners — Make sure your mobile phone is always on, and have your own bag of essentials packed and ready (including toiletries, snacks, a phone charger, and a change of clothes).
10 tips for birth partners — Your comfort and reassurance matters, especially as the contractions get stronger.
10 tips for birth partners — Keep up the words of encouragement, but don't be offended if you get asked to stop talking!

10 tips for birth partners — Try to help your partner focus on something during the contractions - this could be on relaxation or breathing techniques, a spot on the wall, or the baby’s ultrasound picture.
10 tips for birth partners — Help your partner to move about, change positions, or lean on you if that's more comfortable.
10 tips for birth partners — Make sure your partner stays hydrated and keeps up their energy with snacks.
10 tips for birth partners — You may need to help explain to the midwife or doctor what your partner needs or wants.
10 tips for birth partners — You are doing a very important job, so have plenty of snacks and drinks to keep your own energy levels up.
10 tips for birth partners — Take a short break when you can.

Standardy opieki okołoporodowej — 7 maja 2026 r. weszły w życie przepisy nowego standardu organizacyjnego opieki okołoporodowej, który obejmuje organizację opieki sprawowanej nad kobietą w ciąży, kobietą rodzącą, kobietą w połogu oraz nad noworodkiem.
Standardy opieki okołoporodowej — Standard, powinien realnie poprawić komfort, bezpieczeństwo, poszanowanie praw pacjentek oraz jakość opieki okołoporodowej.
Standardy opieki okołoporodowej — Jego przepisy obowiązują wszystkie podmioty wykonujące działalność leczniczą udzielające świadczeń zdrowotnych w zakresie opieki okołoporodowej.

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — edukację przedporodową od momentu stwierdzenia ciąży , która obejmuje praktyczne i teoretyczne przygotowanie kobiety w ciąży oraz ojca dziecka mającego się urodzić lub innej osoby bliskiej do sprawowania opieki nad noworodkiem i niemowlęciem,
Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — większą świadomość i korzystanie ze szczepień zalecanych dla kobiet w ciąży (szczepienia przeciw grypie, krztuścowi, profilaktyka zakażeń RSV),
Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — większą samodzielność położnych w prowadzeniu ciąży fizjologicznej w przypadku braku czynników ryzyka,

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — zwiększenie dostępności do łagodzenia bólu porodowego różnymi metodami farmakologicznymi , przez zobowiązanie podmiotów leczniczych prowadzących szpital do zapewnienia dostępu do co najmniej jednej metody farmakologicznego łagodzenia bólu każdej kobiecie rodzącej oraz wprowadzenie obowiązku publikowania przez podmioty lecznicze informacji o dostępnych w podmiocie metodach łagodzenia bólu porodowego na swojej stronie internetowej i regularną jej aktualizację,
Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — zwrócenie większej uwagi na oczekiwania i preferencje kobiety rodzącej zawarte w planie porodu,

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — możliwość wcześniejszego zapoznania się z wybranym miejscem porodu i dostępnymi w nim metodami łagodzenia bólu porodowego oraz konsultacji anestezjologicznej na wypadek oczekiwanego przez kobietę zastosowania podczas porodu analgezji regionalnej,
Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — możliwość spożywania w czasie porodu posiłków oraz przyjmowania płynów po konsultacji z osobą sprawującą opiekę,
Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — wspiera karmienie piersią przez zapewnienie właściwej organizacji i warunków prawidłowej laktacji i odżywiania noworodka,

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — odpowiednie warunki pobytu w szpitalu, które zapobiegną pogłębianiu traumy u kobiet w sytuacjach szczególnych (poronienie, urodzenie dziecka martwego, niezdolnego do życia lub obarczonego letalnymi schorzeniami, urodzenie chorego dziecka lub dziecka z wadami wrodzonymi, jak również kobiet, które podjęły decyzję o pozostawieniu dziecka w szpitalu),

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — opiekę położnej podstawowej opieki zdrowotnej w miejscu zamieszkania albo pobytu również dla dzieci urodzonych przedwcześnie lub długotrwale hospitalizowanych, kobiet w okresie połogu, również w sytuacji, gdy ich dziecko jest długotrwale hospitalizowane po urodzeniu, kobiet w sytuacji szczególnej,

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — wprowadza konieczne zmiany w świadczeniach profilaktycznych i działaniach w zakresie promocji zdrowia oraz badaniach diagnostycznych i konsultacjach medycznych u kobiet w okresie ciąży,
Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — ochronę przed przemocą domową przypominając personelowi medycznemu o obowiązku wszczęciu procedury „Niebieskie Karty”, w przypadku podejrzenia przemocy domowej,

Standard powinien zapewniać m.in.: — zwrócenie uwagi na konieczność zapewnienia dostępu do świadczeń kobietom ze szczególnymi potrzebami (dostępność architektoniczną, cyfrową, informacyjno-komunikacyjną i w miarę możliwości sprzęt niezbędny do realizacji świadczeń dostosowany do osób ze szczególnymi potrzebami).
Podstawa prawna — Rozporządzenie Ministra Zdrowia z dnia 23 października 2025 r. zmieniające rozporządzenie w sprawie standardu organizacyjnego opieki okołoporodowej Dz.U. 2025 poz. 1525
Mastitis is when your breast becomes swollen, hot and painful.
It is most common in breastfeeding women and does not usually need medical treatment.
Symptoms of mastitis — Mastitis usually only affects 1 breast, and symptoms often come on quickly. They include:
Symptoms of mastitis — a swollen area on your breast that may feel hot and painful to touch – the area may become red but this can be harder to see if you have black or brown skin
Symptoms of mastitis — a wedge-shaped breast lump or a hard area on your breast
Symptoms of mastitis — a burning pain in your breast that might be constant or only when you breastfeed
Symptoms of mastitis — nipple discharge , which may be white or contain streaks of blood
Symptoms of mastitis — You may also get flu -like symptoms, such as aches, a high temperature (or feeling hot, cold or shivery) and tiredness.
Do — if you are breastfeeding, continue to breastfeed your baby when they want and for as long as they want. You can also offer your baby a breastfeed if your breasts are uncomfortably full
Do — hand express enough breast milk to feed your baby if breastfeeding is too painful, or if your baby does not want to feed from your affected breast
Do — when breastfeeding make sure your baby is positioned and attached properly . Your midwife, health visitor or a breastfeeding specialist can advise you.
Do — breast pain may be soothed by applying a cold compress (for example a cloth soaked in cold water) to the affected breast for 10 minutes every hour
Do — take paracetamol or ibuprofen to reduce any pain or high temperature
Do — wear a comfortable and supportive bra
Don’t — do not wear tight-fitting clothing or bras until you feel better
Don’t — do not take aspirin
Don’t — do not express more milk than your baby needs
Don’t — do not apply firm pressure to the breast - any pressure should be gentle
Don’t — do not stop breastfeeding suddenly – find out how to stop breastfeeding
Don’t — do not apply oils, soaks or creams to your breast
Non-urgent advice: See a GP if: — your symptoms do not get better 12 to 24 hours after treating it at home
Non-urgent advice: See a GP if: — your symptoms do not get better 48 hours after taking antibiotics
Non-urgent advice: See a GP if: — you get mastitis and you are not breastfeeding
Treatment for mastitis from a GP — A GP will usually prescribe antibiotics if you have mastitis and your symptoms are not getting better.

Treatment for mastitis from a GP — If you're breastfeeding a very small amount of the antibiotic may go into your breast milk. There is no risk to your baby, but it might make them irritable and restless.
What to do if mastitis comes back — If you are breastfeeding and keep getting mastitis, it might be due to problems with positioning and attaching .
What to do if mastitis comes back — If you have any breastfeeding problems , it's important to ask for help from a midwife, health visitor or a breastfeeding specialist as soon as possible.
What to do if mastitis comes back — You can also call the National Breastfeeding Helpline 24 hours a day on 0300 100 0212
Causes of mastitis — Mastitis is common in breastfeeding women as it can be caused by a build-up of milk.
Causes of mastitis — Women who are not breastfeeding can also get mastitis, as can men. This can be caused by:
Causes of mastitis — smoking – toxins found in tobacco can damage breast tissue
Causes of mastitis — damage to the nipple, such as a piercing or skin condition such as eczema
Causes of mastitis — having a breast implant
Causes of mastitis — having a weakened immune system due to a health condition such as diabetes
Causes of mastitis — shaving or plucking hairs from around your nipples

Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — Opieka perinatalna, czyli okołoporodowa to wielodyscyplinarne działanie, którego celem jest zapewnienie opieki medycznej kobiecie w ciąży i dbałość o rozwój płodu i noworodka do pierwszego roku życia

Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — W opiece okołoporodowej mieści się promocja zdrowia, planowanie rodziny, opieka przedkoncepcyjna, wykrywanie zagrożeń dla matki i płodu oraz opieka medyczna w czasie ciąży, porodu i połogu. Obejmuje również opiekę nad dzieckiem do pierwszego roku życia.
Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — Opieką zajmują się:
Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — lekarze perinatolodzy, położnicy
Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — neonatolodzy
Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — wykwalifikowane położne.

Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — Perinatologia to dziedzina medycyny, która zajmuje się kobietą ciężarną, płodem i noworodkiem, ich fizjologią, diagnostyką i leczeniem schorzeń. Zwana jest medycyną matczyno-płodową. Jest podspecjalnością położnictwa.

Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — Neonatolog jest lekarzem specjalistą, który zajmuje się profilaktyką, diagnozowaniem i leczeniem schorzeń u noworodków, czyli dzieci od urodzenia do pierwszego miesiąca życia i niemowlętami (do 1 roku). Szczególnie jeśli są to wcześniaki, dzieci chore, urodzone z wadami.
Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — Dbaj o siebie szczególnie, gdy jesteś w ciąży. Nie zapominaj o profilaktyce. Bądź w stałym kontakcie z lekarzem prowadzącym. Wybierz położną i korzystaj z jej pomocy.
Czym jest opieka okołoporodowa — Przeczytaj magazyn „Ze Zdrowiem” nr 18 pt. „Ciąża i opieka okołoporodowa” .

Ginekologia i położnictwo — Ginekologia zajmuje się diagnozowaniem, leczeniem i zapobieganiem chorobom narządów rozrodczych kobiet, edukacją na temat higieny od dojrzewania do wieku pomenopeuzalnego. Położnictwo obejmuje również opiekę okołoporodową. Wielu lekarzy specjalizuje się zarówno w położnictwie, jak i w ginekologii.

Ginekologia i położnictwo — Jeśli podejrzewasz, że jesteś w ciąży, jak najszybciej skontaktuj się z wybranym przez Ciebie lekarzem położnikiem. Nie później niż w 7-8 tygodniu od ustania miesiączki. Lekarz będzie prowadził Twoją ciążę aż do porodu i skontroluje Twój stan zdrowia podczas połogu.
Ginekologia i położnictwo — Położnictwo dotyczy wszystkich aspektów ciąży. Ginekolog położnik zajmuje się m.in:
Ginekologia i położnictwo — opieką prenatalną
Ginekologia i położnictwo — przyjmowaniem porodu
Ginekologia i położnictwo — opieką okołoporodową
Ginekologia i położnictwo — może też pomóc w zajściu w ciążę, zlecając odpowiednie badania i terapii
Ginekologia i położnictwo — diagnozuje i leczy powikłania ciąży i zagrożenia płodu
Ginekologia i położnictwo — może zalecić poród przez cesarskie cięcie.

Ginekologia i położnictwo — Od okresu dojrzewania raz w roku powinnaś zgłaszać się do lekarza ginekologa na kontrolne badania, nawet jeśli nic Ci nie dolega. Podczas ciąży będziesz się częściej spotykała z lekarzem.
Ginekologia i położnictwo — Nie musisz mieć skierowania do ginekologa i możesz wybrać dowolnego lekarza.

Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — Położna jest częścią zespołu medycznego, nie podlega bezpośrednio lekarzowi. Jest członkiem zespołu terapeutycznego. Świadczy pomoc położniczo-ginekologiczną kobietom w każdym wieku. Szczególnie znana jest jej pomoc w okresie ciąży, połogu i laktacji.
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — Położna zajmuje się m.in.:
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — profilaktyką chorób kobiecych i patologii położniczych
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — edukacją w zakresie szczepień
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — przygotowaniem do porodu
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — zapobieganiem chorobom przenoszonym drogą płciową
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — opieką nad kobietami po przebytej operacji ginekologicznej, onkologicznej.

Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — Zachęca do regularnych badań profilaktycznych: cytologii, samobadania piersi, USG piersi, mammografii, czy profilaktycznego USG narządów rodnych. Jeśli ma umowę z NFZ, może wykonać także cytologię.
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — Wizytę możesz umówić w swojej przychodni POZ lub w gabinecie położnej POZ. Dowiedz się, jak możesz wybrać położną .

Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — Gdy jesteś w ciąży, jak najszybciej wybierz położną i skontaktuj się z nią. Będzie się Tobą opiekowała w ciąży i w połogu. Zadba także o dziecko do drugiego miesiąca życia. Pomoże Ci w karmieniu.

Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — KTG – kardiotokografia to badanie, które monitoruje w nieinwazyjny sposób jednocześnie czynność serca płodu i skurcze macicy. Pozwala oceniać stan dziecka przed i w trakcie porodu. Laktacja – wydzielanie mleka matki, pojawia się po porodzie i trwa przez okres karmienia piersią.
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — Zadania położnej POZ obejmują kompleksową pielęgnacyjną opiekę położniczo-neonatologiczno ginekologiczną, w tym:
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — edukację na temat planowania rodziny
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — opiekę nad kobietą od 21. tygodnia ciąży do porodu
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — badania KTG i USG
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — opiekę nad kobietą, noworodkiem i niemowlęciem do ukończenia 2. miesiąca życia – wizyty patronażowe
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — konsultacje laktacyjne, wsparcie w problemach z karmieniem

Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — opiekę w chorobach ginekologicznych, po operacji ginekologicznej lub onkologiczno--ginekologicznej do całkowitego zagojenia się rany pooperacyjnej – potrzebujesz skierowania ze szpitala
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — zastrzyki i zabiegi zlecone przez lekarzy w gabinecie położnej i w domu pacjenta
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — pobieranie materiału z szyjki macicy do przesiewowego badania cytologicznego w ramach Programu profilaktyki raka szyjki macicy, o ile ma umowę z NFZ
Położna – jej rola w życiu kobiety — opiekę nad kobietą w każdym okresie jej życia.

Opieka położnej podczas ciąży i połogu — Kobieta ciężarna ma prawo do bezpłatnej opieki okołoporodowej od 21. tygodnia ciąży oraz w połogu – do 8. tygodnia życia dziecka. Niezależnie od opieki lekarza czy zajęć w tzw. „szkole rodzenia”.
Opieka położnej podczas ciąży i połogu — W ciąży możesz mieć 26 spotkań z położną POZ, w dogodnych dla obu terminach. Położna pracuje od poniedziałku do piątku od 8:00 do 18:00.
Opieka położnej podczas ciąży i połogu — Położna POZ zapewni Ci edukację przedporodową:
Opieka położnej podczas ciąży i połogu — od 21. do 31. tygodnia ciąży – 1 raz w tygodniu, maksymalnie 10 wizyt
Opieka położnej podczas ciąży i połogu — od 32. tygodnia ciąży – 2 razy w tygodniu, maksymalnie 16 wizyt.
Wizyty patronażowe — Wizyty patronażowe mają na celu monitorowanie stanu zdrowia matki i noworodka, ocenę rozwoju dziecka.
Wizyty patronażowe — Do 2 miesięcy życia dziecka położna POZ jest zobowiązana do 4–6 wizyt patronażowych.
Wizyty patronażowe — Pierwsza wizyta odbywa się nie później niż 48 godzin po opuszczeniu szpitala przez matkę i dziecko. Opieka nad noworodkiem lub niemowlęciem obejmuje m.in.:
Wizyty patronażowe — obserwację stanu skóry, błon śluzowych, pępka, wydalin, wydzielin, rozwoju psychoruchowego, funkcjonowania narządów zmysłów.
Wizyty patronażowe — Położna edukuje rodziców na temat:
Wizyty patronażowe — pielęgnacji noworodka, karmienia piersią, laktacji, badań profilaktycznych, opieki medycznej i socjalnej, laktacji.

Wizyty patronażowe — Po zakończeniu wizyt patronażowych położna przekazuje opiekę nad niemowlęciem pielęgniarce podstawowej opieki zdrowotnej (POZ). Nadal jednak opiekuje się mamą, której udziela wsparcia w zakresie karmienia piersią.

Nowe uprawnienia w opiece okołoporodowej — Nowe rozporządzenie wprowadza zmiany w opiece okołoporodowej. Wchodzi w życie od maja 2026 roku. Rozporządzenie między innymi zwraca uwagę na podmiotowe traktowanie kobiet rodzących, współpracę z personelem medycznym i respektowanie praw pacjenta. Zapewnia także jednolity sposób postępowania wobec kobiety w okresie okołoporodowym i jej dziecka bez względu na miejsce zamieszkania. Zwiększa też rolę położnej.
Nowe uprawnienia w opiece okołoporodowej — Zmiany w r ozporządzeniu w sprawie standardu organizacyjnego opieki okołoporodowej , wchodzą w życie po 6 miesiącach od dnia ogłoszenia 6.11.2025.

Know the signs — There are several signs that labour might be starting, including:
Know the signs — contractions or tightenings
Know the signs — a "show", when the plug of mucus from your cervix (entrance to your womb, or uterus) comes away
Know the signs — an urge to go to the toilet, which is caused by your baby's head pressing on your bowel
Know the signs — your waters breaking
When to contact your midwife or maternity unit — Call your midwife or maternity unit for guidance if:
When to contact your midwife or maternity unit — you think you’re in labour
When to contact your midwife or maternity unit — you’re having regular contractions coming every 5 minutes or more often
When to contact your midwife or maternity unit — You can also call your midwife or maternity unit if you’re unsure or worried about anything.
When to contact your midwife or maternity unit — Call 111 if you’re unable to contact your midwife or maternity unit.
Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — your waters break
Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — you have vaginal bleeding
Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — your baby is moving less than usual
Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — you're less than 37 weeks pregnant and think you might be in labour
Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — any of your contractions last longer than 2 minutes
Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — you're having 6 or more contractions every 10 minutes

Urgent advice: Call your midwife or maternity unit urgently if: — These signs mean you need to see a midwife or doctor. Do not wait until the next day – call immediately, even if it's the middle of the night.
Immediate action required: Call 999 and ask for an ambulance if: — you think your baby is coming now and you have a strong urge to push

Latent phase of labour — The start of labour is called the latent phase. This is when your cervix becomes soft and thin, and starts opening for your baby to be born. This can take hours or sometimes days.
Latent phase of labour — You'll probably be advised to stay at home during this time. If you go to the hospital or maternity unit, they may suggest you go back home.
Latent phase of labour — Find out more about the stages of labour and what you can do at home during the latent phase.
Latent phase of labour — Call your midwife if you're unsure or worried about anything.
What do contractions feel like — When you have a contraction, your womb tightens and then relaxes. For some people, contractions may feel like extreme period pains.

What do contractions feel like — You may have had ‘practice contractions’ during your pregnancy, particularly towards the end. These tightenings are called Braxton Hicks contractions, which may feel uncomfortable, but are usually painless. Braxton Hicks contractions generally do not last that long, do not happen very frequently and do not build up.

What do contractions feel like — Your contractions tend to become longer, stronger and more frequent as your labour progresses. During a contraction, your womb muscles tighten and the pain increases. If you put your hand on your abdomen, you'll feel it getting harder. When the muscles relax, the pain fades and you’ll feel the hardness ease.
What do contractions feel like — The contractions are pushing your baby down and opening the entrance to your womb (the cervix), ready for your baby to go through.
What do contractions feel like — Your midwife will probably advise you to stay at home until your contractions become frequent.
Backache often comes on in labour — You may get backache or a heavy, aching feeling.

A "show" can signal the start of labour — During pregnancy, there's a plug of mucus in your cervix. This mucus comes away just before labour starts, or when in early labour, and it may pass out of your vagina. This sticky, jelly-like pink mucus is called a show.
A "show" can signal the start of labour — It may come away in 1 blob or in several pieces. It's pink because it contains a small amount of blood.
A "show" can signal the start of labour — If you're losing more blood, it may be a sign something is wrong, so phone your hospital or midwife straight away.
A "show" can signal the start of labour — A show indicates that the cervix is starting to open. Labour may quickly follow or may take a few days. Sometimes there is no show.
What happens when my waters break — It's likely your waters will break during labour, but it can also happen before labour starts.

What happens when my waters break — Your baby develops and grows inside a bag of fluid called the amniotic sac. When it's time for your baby to be born, the sac usually breaks and the amniotic fluid drains out through your vagina. This is your waters breaking. Sometimes when you're in labour, a midwife or doctor may offer to break your waters.

What happens when my waters break — If your waters break naturally, you may feel a slow trickle or a sudden gush of water you cannot control. To prepare for this, you could keep a period pad (but not a tampon) handy if you're going out, and put a protective sheet on your bed.

What happens when my waters break — Amniotic fluid is clear and pale. Sometimes it's difficult to tell amniotic fluid from urine. When your waters break, the water may be a little bloodstained to begin with.
What happens when my waters break — Tell your midwife immediately if:
What happens when my waters break — the waters are smelly or coloured
What happens when my waters break — you're losing blood
What happens when my waters break — This could mean you and your baby need urgent attention.
What happens when my waters break — If your waters break before labour starts, call your midwife. Use a period pad (not a tampon) so your midwife can check the colour of the waters.

If labour does not start after your waters break — It's usual to go into labour within 24 hours of the waters breaking. You'll be offered an induction if you do not because, without amniotic fluid, there's a small increased risk of infection for your baby.
If labour does not start after your waters break — Until your induction, or if you choose to wait for labour to start naturally, tell your midwife immediately if:
If labour does not start after your waters break — your baby moves less than usual
If labour does not start after your waters break — there's any change in the colour or smell of any fluid coming from your vagina

If labour does not start after your waters break — You should take your temperature every 4 hours when you're awake, and tell your midwife if it's raised. A raised temperature is usually above 37.5C, but you may need to call before this – check with your midwife.
If labour does not start after your waters break — There's no evidence that having a bath or shower after your waters have broken increases your risk of infection, but having sex might.
How to cope when labour begins — At the beginning of labour, you can:
How to cope when labour begins — walk or move about, if you feel like it
How to cope when labour begins — drink fluids – you may find sports (isotonic) drinks help keep your energy levels up
How to cope when labour begins — have a snack, if you feel like it

How to cope when labour begins — try any relaxation and breathing exercises you've learned to deal with contractions as they get stronger and more painful – your birth partner can help by doing these with you
How to cope when labour begins — have your birth partner rub your back – this can help relieve pain
How to cope when labour begins — take paracetamol according to the instructions on the packet – paracetamol is safe to take in labour
How to cope when labour begins — have a warm bath

There are no rules about when to start having sex again after you have given birth.
You'll probably feel sore as well as tired after your baby is born, so don't rush into it.
If sex hurts, it won't be pleasurable. You may want to use a personal lubricant, available from pharmacies, to begin with.
Hormonal changes after birth can make your vagina feel drier than usual.
You may be worried about changes to your body or getting pregnant again. Men may worry about hurting their partner.
It might be some time before you want to have sex. Until then, both of you can carry on being loving and close in other ways.
If you or your partner have any worries, talk about them together. You can talk with your health visitor or GP if you need some more help.

Tips for starting sex again after birth — If penetration hurts, say so. If you pretend that everything's all right when it isn't, you may start to see sex as a nuisance or unpleasant, rather than a pleasure. You can still give each other pleasure without penetration – for example, by mutual masturbation.

Tips for starting sex again after birth — Take it gently. Perhaps explore with your own fingers first to reassure yourself that sex won't hurt. Hormonal changes after childbirth may mean you may need to use lubricant to help make sex more comfortable.
Tips for starting sex again after birth — Make time to relax together. You're more likely to make love when your minds are on each other rather than other things.
Tips for starting sex again after birth — Get help if you need it. If you're still experiencing pain when you have your postnatal check , talk to your GP.
Contraception after having a baby — You can get pregnant 3 weeks after the birth of a baby, including if you're breastfeeding and your periods haven't started again.
Contraception after having a baby — You need to use contraception every time you have sex after giving birth unless you want to get pregnant again.
Contraception after having a baby — Your midwife will discuss contraception with you after your baby is born.
Contraception after having a baby — You can talk to your GP, health visitor or sexual health clinic (sometimes called a family planning clinic) about contraception at any time.
Contraception after having a baby — It's usually recommended that you wait at least 12 months after giving birth before becoming pregnant again.
Contraception after having a baby — This is because getting pregnant sooner may increase the risk of some health issues, such as having a baby with a low birth weight.
Contraception after having a baby — If you do become pregnant, there are things you can do to help you stay as healthy as possible.
Your contraception choices — You can start using some types of contraception immediately after giving birth. For some other types, it’s recommended to wait for a few weeks.
Contraception choices straight after birth — You can start these types of contraception straight after the birth, including if you’re breastfeeding:
Contraception choices straight after birth — contraceptive implant
Contraception choices straight after birth — contraceptive injection
Contraception choices straight after birth — progestogen-only pill
Contraception choices straight after birth — female (internal) condoms
Contraception choices straight after birth — IUD (coil) or IUS (hormonal coil)
Contraception choices straight after birth — If an IUD or IUS is not fitted within 48 hours of giving birth, it’s recommended to wait until 4 weeks after the birth.

Contraception choices 3 weeks after the birth — If you’re not breastfeeding and a healthcare professional has checked you have no risk factors for a blood clot, you can start to use these methods 3 weeks after the birth:
Contraception choices 3 weeks after the birth — combined pill
Contraception choices 3 weeks after the birth — vaginal ring
Contraception choices 3 weeks after the birth — contraceptive patch
Contraception choices 3 weeks after the birth — If you’re breastfeeding, you’ll usually be advised to wait until at least 6 weeks after the birth before starting the combined pill, ring or patch.
Contraception choices 6 weeks after birth — You can usually start using a diaphragm or cap around 6 weeks after the birth.

Contraception choices 6 weeks after birth — If you used a diaphragm or cap before the birth, see a doctor or nurse at a contraception clinic to make sure it still fits correctly. You may need a new size.
Contraception choices 6 weeks after birth — If you’re breastfeeding, you should discuss whether the combined pill, vaginal ring or patch is suitable for you with your nurse or doctor.
Contraception and breastfeeding — You're unlikely to have any periods if you breastfeed exclusively (give your baby breast milk only) and your baby is under 6 months old.
Contraception and breastfeeding — Because of this, some women use breastfeeding as a form of natural contraception. This is known as the lactational amenorrhoea method, or LAM.
Contraception and breastfeeding — Find out about natural family planning, including LAM .
Contraception and breastfeeding — It's important to start using another form of contraception if:
Contraception and breastfeeding — your baby is more than 6 months old
Contraception and breastfeeding — you give them anything else apart from breast milk, such as a dummy, formula or solid foods
Contraception and breastfeeding — your periods start again (even light spotting counts)
Contraception and breastfeeding — you stop night feeding
Contraception and breastfeeding — you start to breastfeed less often
Contraception and breastfeeding — there are longer intervals between feeds, both during the day and at night
Contraception and breastfeeding — The effect of expressing breast milk on LAM isn't known, but it may make it less effective.

Uzyskaj Kartę Dużej Rodziny — Masz troje dzieci lub więcej? Twoja rodzina może korzystać z Karty Dużej Rodziny, niezależnie od dochodu w rodzinie .
Uzyskaj Kartę Dużej Rodziny — Karta ta daje zniżki na różne towary i usługi – na przykład przejazdy kolejowe, kulturę i sport. Dowiedz się, jak uzyskać kartę.

Uzyskaj Kartę Dużej Rodziny — Kartę Dużej Rodziny możesz też wyświetlać w aplikacji mObywatel . Nie musisz składać wniosku o kartę plastikową – możesz korzystać tylko z karty elektronicznej (mobilnej).

Kto może uzyskać — który mieszka w Polsce,
Kto może uzyskać — ojciec i matka,
Kto może uzyskać — macocha lub ojczym (małżonek jednego z rodziców),
Kto może uzyskać — Kartę Dużej Rodziny mogą dostać tylko rodzice:
Kto może uzyskać — którzy nie są i nie byli pozbawieni – w stosunku do co najmniej trojga dzieci – władzy rodzicielskiej,
Kto może uzyskać — których władza rodzicielska nie została ograniczona przez umieszczenie dziecka w pieczy zastępczej.
Kto może uzyskać — Jeśli nie masz już na utrzymaniu co najmniej trojga dzieci, kartę otrzymasz tylko ty i drugi rodzic lub małżonek rodzica.
Kto może uzyskać — Kartę może też uzyskać rodzic (rodzice) zastępczy lub osoba (osoby), która prowadzi rodzinny dom dziecka.
Co musisz przygotować — wniosek o przyznanie Karty Dużej Rodziny – szczegóły znajdziesz w sekcji Co musisz zrobić ,

Co musisz przygotować — oświadczenie – ojciec i matka oświadczają, że nie są pozbawieni władzy rodzicielskiej ani ograniczeni we władzy rodzicielskiej przez umieszczenie dziecka w pieczy zastępczej w stosunku do co najmniej trojga dzieci. Napisz to oświadczenie samodzielnie lub wypełnij formularz oświadczenia o władzy rodzicielskiej ,
Co musisz przygotować — dowód osobisty lub paszport – jeśli nie masz numeru PESEL,
Co musisz przygotować — dowód osobisty lub paszport i akt małżeństwa – jeśli jesteś macochą lub ojczymem (małżonkiem jednego z rodziców) i nie masz numeru PESEL,
Co musisz przygotować — akt urodzenia albo dowód osobisty lub paszport dzieci poniżej 18 lat – jeśli nie mają numeru PESEL,
Co musisz przygotować — dowód osobisty lub paszport dzieci powyżej 18 lat – jeśli nie mają numeru PESEL,

Co musisz przygotować — oświadczenie o planowanym terminie ukończenia przez dzieci powyżej 18 lat nauki w szkole lub na studiach – napisz je samodzielnie lub wypełnij formularz oświadczenia o planowanym terminie ukończenia nauki w szkole lub szkole wyższej ,
Co musisz przygotować — dowód osobisty lub paszport dzieci z niepełnosprawnością powyżej 18 lat – jeśli nie mają numeru PESEL,
Co musisz przygotować — postanowienie o umieszczeniu dzieci w rodzinie zastępczej albo rodzinnym domu dziecka,
Co musisz przygotować — oświadczenie o pozostawaniu dzieci w dotychczasowej rodzinie zastępczej albo rodzinnym domu dziecka,
Co musisz przygotować — dokument, który potwierdzi prawo cudzoziemca do mieszkania w Polsce,
Co musisz przygotować — pobytu stałego,
Co musisz przygotować — pobytu rezydenta długoterminowego Unii Europejskiej,

Co musisz przygotować — Kartę możesz też wyświetlać w aplikacji mObywatel.

Co musisz przygotować — Możesz zrezygnować z wnioskowania o kartę tradycyjną i korzystać tylko z karty elektronicznej. We wniosku możesz wskazać, czy rodzice będą mogli wyświetlać w aplikacji mObywatel tylko swoje karty, czy także karty pozostałych członków rodziny.

Zakażenia wywołane RSV — Syncytialny wirus oddechowy (RSV - respiratory syncytial virus) to powszechny wirus układu oddechowego, który powoduje zazwyczaj łagodne objawy przypominające przeziębienie. RSV może dotknąć osoby w każdym wieku, a prawie wszystkie dzieci zostaną zakażone wirusem RSV przed ukończeniem drugiego roku życia. Pomimo tego, że większość przypadków jest łagodna (osoby zakażone wirusem RSV zwykle wracają do zdrowia w ciągu około tygodnia bez konieczności leczenia), RSV może zaostrzyć istniejące schorzenia i powodować poważne komplikacje, które mogą zagrażać życiu. Najbardziej zagrożone są wcześniaki i dzieci poniżej szóstego miesiąca życia, osoby powyżej 65 roku życia oraz osoby z osłabionym układem odpornościowym lub istniejącymi wcześniej schorzeniami, takimi jak cukrzyca, choroby serca i choroby płuc.
Drogi zakażenia — RSV przenosi się z osoby na osobę drogą kropelkową, gdy zakażona osoba oddycha, mówi, kaszle lub kicha.
Drogi zakażenia — RSV może również rozprzestrzeniać się poprzez kontakt bezpośredni z osobą zakażoną jak również poprzez kontakt pośredni z powierzchniami, czy przedmiotami, skażonymi wirusem.
Objawy — Objawy pojawiają się zwykle od dwóch do ośmiu dni po zakażeniu i najczęściej obejmują kaszel, kichanie, gorączkę, katar, świszczący oddech, ból gardła, ból głowy, zmęczenie.
Objawy — U niemowląt zakażonych wirusem RSV mogą wystąpić objawy, takie jak drażliwość, utrata apetytu, zmiany w sposobie oddychania, bezdech (szczególnie podczas snu).
Objawy — U dzieci poniżej 5 roku życia wirus RSV może również powodować przyspieszony oddech, problemy z połykaniem czy sepsę.
Objawy — Dorośli mogą natomiast doświadczać również dezorientacji i duszności.
Objawy — Powikłania ciężkiego zakażenia RSV obejmują zapalenie oskrzelików, zapalenie małych dróg oddechowych w płucach i zapalenie płuc.

Objawy — Krótkie, płytkie oddechy, rozszerzenie nozdrzy podczas wdechu, głośny oddech, przerwy w oddychaniu i zapadanie się klatki piersiowej oznaczają potrzebę pilnej opieki medycznej. Ponadto rodzice powinni zwrócić uwagę na niebieskie lub szare zabarwienie ust lub paznokci, ponieważ jest to oznaka krytycznie niskiego poziomu tlenu we krwi.
Objawy — U niemowląt może również rozwinąć się sepsa, infekcja układu krwionośnego, która może powodować różne objawy, w tym spadek ciśnienia krwi, przyspieszenie akcji serca i gorączkę.

Objawy — W UE, Norwegii i Wielkiej Brytanii wirus RSV jest odpowiedzialny za hospitalizację około 213 000 dzieci poniżej piątego roku życia, z których niektóre wymagają intensywnej terapii, oraz około 158 000 dorosłych każdego roku. Co roku jedna na dwadzieścia osób starszych w Europie zapada na RSV.
Leczenie — Łagodne przypadki infekcji RSV zwykle nie wymagają leczenia, ponieważ chorzy wracają do zdrowia po kilku dniach.

Leczenie — U niemowląt i małych dzieci objawy ciężkiego zakażenia RSV, które wymagają pilnej pomocy medycznej, są związane z trudnościami w oddychaniu. Leczenie szpitalne może obejmować opiekę wspomagającą, podanie leków przeciwwirusowych, wspomaganie oddychania, a także leczenie powikłań, które mogą się pojawić.

Zapobieganie — Podstawowe środki zapobiegawcze są takie same jak w przypadku większości innych wirusów układu oddechowego. Obejmują one unikanie bliskiego kontaktu z osobami chorymi, częste mycie lub dezynfekcję rąk, unikanie dotykania oczu, nosa lub ust, utrzymywanie właściwej higieny dróg oddechowych i etykiety kaszlu.
Zapobieganie — Jednak najskuteczniejszą formą zapobiegania infekcjom wywołanym przez RSV są szczepienia ochronne.

Szczepienia — W 2023 r. Unia Europejska zatwierdziła pierwszą szczepionkę przeciwko RSV odpowiednią do ochrony niemowląt w wieku do sześciu miesięcy, a także dwie szczepionki dla osób starszych. Po podaniu matce w czasie ciąży przeciwciała wytworzone w odpowiedzi na szczepionkę mogą przenikać przez łożysko do płodu, chroniąc dziecko przez okres do sześciu miesięcy po urodzeniu. Szczepienia kobiet w ciąży przeciwko RSV należy wykonać między 24 – 36 tygodniem ciąży (optymalnie w 32 – 36 tygodniu ciąży) i są one bezpłatne.
Szczepienia — Osoby w wieku 65 lat i starsze mogą otrzymać szczepionkę przeciw RSV bezpłatnie, natomiast dla osób w wieku 60–64 lata jest ona refundowana w wysokości 50%.
It's recommended to buy a baby car seat before your baby is born if possible. It's important to buy a seat that fits your car and is suitable for a newborn.
If you have your baby in hospital or a birth centre, you will need the car seat to drive your newborn home safely. It's a good idea to practise fitting the seat before your baby is born.

Tips for buying a baby car seat — When buying a car seat, it's best to try a few in your car before making a decision. Try to find a retailer who is willing to help you with this. Ask whether staff have been trained in fitting car seats.

Tips for buying a baby car seat — Check whether your car has Isofix connectors built into it. These are designed to make fitting baby and child car seats simpler. Most modern family cars have them. They may be hidden in the cracks between the padding of your car seats.
Tips for buying a baby car seat — If your baby is likely to travel in another car regularly – for example, with other family members – check the car seat fits their car, too.
Tips for buying a baby car seat — Some car seat manufacturers have online guides showing which cars their seats will fit in.
Tips for buying a baby car seat — Always choose a baby or child car seat that's right for your child's current height and weight.

Tips for buying a baby car seat — Do not buy a secondhand car seat. It could have been damaged in an accident, and may not have all its parts, including the instructions. It may also not be the safest and most user-friendly model, plus it may not fit your car properly.
Tips for buying a baby car seat — Only accept a car seat from friends or family if you know its history, it's not too old and it comes with instructions.

Tips for buying a baby car seat — Think about how you will be using the car seat. If you'll be lifting your baby in and out of the car a lot, for example, you may be better off getting a lightweight seat with a base that stays in the car.
Tips for buying a baby car seat — All car seats in this country should be EU-approved. Look for the "E" mark label on the seat.
What are i-Size car seats? — i-Size is a European safety standard for baby and child car seats. It's part of regulation ECE R129, which will eventually replace the old safety regulation R44/04.
What are i-Size car seats? — The idea is that all car seats will eventually meet the tighter i-Size safety standards.

What are i-Size car seats? — i-Size car seats usually fit into Isofix points in your car, but some seats can be fitted using a seatbelt. It's important to check how the car seat is fitted before you buy it if you do not have an Isofix point in your car.
What are i-Size car seats? — Visit the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) child car seats website for more on i-Size car seats
What size car seat? — You can choose a child car seat based on your child’s height or weight.
Height-based car seats — Height-based seats must be rear facing until your child is 15 months old or over. Once your child is 15 months old or over they can use a forward-facing child car seat.
Height-based car seats — You must check the seat to make sure it’s suitable for your child’s height.
Height-based car seats — Only approved height-based child car seats can be used in the UK. These have a label showing a capital E in a circle and R129.
Weight-based car seats — Car seats are divided into 3 main groups, depending on your baby or child's age and weight

Weight-based car seats — group 0+ – rear-facing car seats suitable for babies aged up to about 15 months or who weigh up to 13kg (29lb); some can be clipped onto a pushchair frame and are known as travel systems
Weight-based car seats — group 1 – rear or forward-facing seats suitable for children who weigh 9kg to 18kg (20lb to 40lb) or who are aged from about 9 months to 4 years
Weight-based car seats — group 2/3 – rear or forward-facing seats suitable for children who weigh 15kg to 36kg (33lb to 5st 9lb) or are aged from about 4 to 11 years

Weight-based car seats — You can also buy combination seats that cross over these groups, such as group 0+/1 seats, which are suitable from birth until your child weighs about 18kg (40lb) or is aged about 4 years.
Weight-based car seats — Use a rear-facing car seat for as long as your child fits into it, as these offer better protection in the event of a car accident.

Baby or child car-seat fitting — It is dangerous and illegal to carry a baby in a rear-facing baby seat in a front passenger seat that has an active airbag. Forward-facing seats in the same position, while not illegal, are not ideal. It's always safer for children to travel in the back of the car.
Baby or child car-seat fitting — Make sure the seat is fitted properly in the car, following the manufacturer's instructions.
Baby or child car-seat fitting — Look out for safety days where experts demonstrate how to fit baby and child car seats safely. These often take place in supermarket or shopping mall car parks.
Using a baby or child car seat — Make sure you always put your baby into their car seat from the pavement side of the car.

Using a baby or child car seat — Make sure your baby is securely strapped in according to the manufacturer's instructions. When you buy your car seat, ask the retail staff to demonstrate how to strap your baby into it.
More help and advice on car seats — The road safety officer at your local council can give you detailed advice about child car seats. You can find your local council on GOV.UK .
More help and advice on car seats — You should be able to get advice from any good car seat retailer or the manufacturer.
More help and advice on car seats — You'll find lots more advice on the RoSPA child car seat safety website
More help and advice on car seats — Visit GOV.UK for information about baby car seats and the law

Key points — Be aware of urgent maternal warning signs and symptoms during pregnancy and in the year after delivery.
Key points — Seek medical care immediately if you experience any signs or symptoms that are listed below.
Key points — The symptoms below can be a sign of a life-threatening condition.
Would you be able to spot an urgent maternal warning sign? — Download Urgent Maternal Warning Signs poster
Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time — Feels like the worst headache of your life.
Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time — Lasts even after treatment with medication and fluid intake.
Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time — Starts suddenly with severe pain—like a clap of thunder.
Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time — Throbs and is on one side of your head above your ear.
Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time — Comes with blurred vision or dizziness.
Dizziness or fainting — You faint or pass out.
Dizziness or fainting — You have dizziness and lightheadedness that's ongoing, or comes and goes over many days.
Dizziness or fainting — You experience a gap in time of which you have no memory.
Changes in your vision — You see flashes of light or bright spots.
Changes in your vision — You have blind spots or you can't see at all for a short time.
Changes in your vision — Your vision is blurry, you can't focus, or you're seeing double.
Fever of 100.4°F or higher — You have a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher.
Extreme swelling of your hands or face — Swelling in your hands makes it hard to bend your fingers or wear rings.
Extreme swelling of your hands or face — Swelling in your face makes it hard to open your eyes all the way—they feel and look puffy.
Extreme swelling of your hands or face — Your lips and mouth feel swollen or you have a loss of feeling.
Thoughts about harming yourself or your baby — Feel very sad, hopeless, or not good enough.
Thoughts about harming yourself or your baby — Don't feel that you have control over your life.
Thoughts about harming yourself or your baby — Feel extremely worried all the time.
Thoughts about harming yourself or your baby — You may think about hurting your baby and/or you may have scary thoughts that come when you don’t want or that are hard to get rid of.
Trouble Breathing — You feel short of breath suddenly or over time, as if you can't breathe deeply enough to get enough air in your lungs.
Trouble Breathing — Your throat and/or chest feel tight.
Trouble Breathing — You have trouble breathing when you're laying down flat, such as needing to prop your head up with pillows to sleep.
Chest pain or fast-beating heart — A feeling of tightness or pressure in the center of your chest.
Chest pain or fast-beating heart — Pain that travels to your back, neck, or arm.
Chest pain or fast-beating heart — A fast heartbeat or a pounding in your chest.
Chest pain or fast-beating heart — An irregular heart rate or skipped heartbeats.
Chest pain or fast-beating heart — You feel dizzy, faint, or disoriented.
Chest pain or fast-beating heart — You have trouble catching your breath (talking and breathing are difficult).
Severe nausea and throwing up — You feel severely sick to your stomach (nauseous) beyond the normal queasy feeling and throwing up that many moms have in early pregnancy.
Severe nausea and throwing up — You are unable to drink for more than 8 hours or eat for more than 24 hours.
Severe nausea and throwing up — You throw up and can't keep water or other fluids in your stomach.
Severe nausea and throwing up — A dry mouth.
Severe nausea and throwing up — Dizziness or lightheadedness.
Severe belly pain that doesn’t go away — You have a sharp, stabbing, or cramp-like belly pain that doesn't go away.
Severe belly pain that doesn’t go away — Your belly pain starts suddenly and is severe, or gets worse over time.
Severe belly pain that doesn’t go away — You have severe chest, shoulder, or back pain.
Baby’s movement stopping or slowing during pregnancy — You feel that your baby has stopped moving or your baby is moving less than before.
Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking during pregnancy — You have any bleeding from your vagina that is more than spotting—like a period.
Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking during pregnancy — You have fluid leaking out of your vagina.
Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking during pregnancy — You have vaginal discharge that smells bad.
Vaginal bleeding or discharge after pregnancy — You have heavy bleeding—soaking through one or more pads in an hour.
Vaginal bleeding or discharge after pregnancy — You pass clots bigger than an egg or you pass tissue.
Severe swelling, redness, or pain of your leg or arm — It may or may not hurt when you touch it.
Severe swelling, redness, or pain of your leg or arm — It may hurt when you flex your foot to stand or walk.
Severe swelling, redness, or pain of your leg or arm — The painful area can also be red, swollen, and warm to the touch.
Severe swelling, redness, or pain of your leg or arm — You have pain, tenderness or swelling in your arm, usually on just one side of your body.
Overwhelming tiredness — You are suddenly very tired and weak, not like chronic fatigue.
Overwhelming tiredness — You don't have enough energy to go about your day.
Overwhelming tiredness — No matter how much you sleep, you don't feel refreshed.
Overwhelming tiredness — You feel so tired that you don't get up to take care of your baby.
Overwhelming tiredness — You feel sad after having your baby.

Overwhelming tiredness — This list is not meant to cover every symptom you might have. If you feel like something just isn't right, or you aren't sure if it's serious, talk to your health care provider. Be sure to tell them if you are pregnant or were pregnant within the last year. This list was developed by the Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health. Learn more about the warning signs by visiting the Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health website.
